ambundu_sun_moon_daughter.name: Bears and mothers the thunder-twins Sudika-Mbambi and Kabundungulu
ambundu_sun_moon_daughter.notes: Daughter of the Sun (Lumbi/Kambonge) and the Moon (Mwesi/Kakwiji); won in marriage by the mortal Nzua dia Kimanaueze, she gives birth to the wonder-children who speak from her womb and are born already armed.

sources.reference: Heli Chatelain, Folk-Tales of Angola (1894), 'The Son of Kimanaueze and the Daughter of the Sun and the Moon'; 'Sudika-Mbambi'

ambundu_kalunga.name: Summons mortals across the Kalunga line to the land of the dead
ambundu_kalunga.notes: As Lord Kalunga-ngombe, King of the Netherworld, he calls the living over the boundary (the sea/river dividing the living from the ancestors) to dwell among the dead.

sources.reference: Alice Werner, Myths and Legends of the Bantu (1933), ch. II 'Where Man Came From, and How Death Came'

ambundu_kalunga.name: Guards the threshold between the world of the living and the dead
ambundu_kalunga.notes: Kalunga is itself the liminal frontier — vast water (sea or river) — that souls must cross to reach the ancestors; the personified Kalunga presides over that passage.

sources.reference: Alice Werner, Myths and Legends of the Bantu (1933)

ambundu_kianda.name: Grants or withholds the fishermen's catch
ambundu_kianda.notes: Patroness of the sea and inland waters; fishermen of Luanda pray to her before setting out for a safe voyage and a full catch.

sources.reference: Heli Chatelain, Folk-Tales of Angola (1894), notes on Kimbundu spirit-beings; Kianda of the Ilha de Luanda

ambundu_kianda.name: Commands the sea, rivers and lakes and may raise or calm their dangers
ambundu_kianda.notes: Each body of water has its own kianda (pl. ianda); she can wreck or spare boats and is propitiated to ward off sea-disasters.

sources.reference: Chatelain, Folk-Tales of Angola (1894)

ambundu_kabundungulu.name: Revives his slain twin from his bones
ambundu_kabundungulu.notes: When the life-tree (kilembe) withered, signalling Sudika-Mbambi's death, Kabundungulu travelled to recover and restore his brother to life.

sources.reference: Heli Chatelain, Folk-Tales of Angola (1894), 'Sudika-Mbambi'

ambundu_nzambi.name: Speaks the cosmos into being and then withdraws
ambundu_nzambi.notes: As supreme creator Nzambi a Mpungu calls the world into existence and orders it, thereafter remaining remote (otiose), with daily affairs delegated to lesser spirits and the ancestors.

sources.reference: Karl Laman, The Kongo (1953-68); Alice Werner, Myths and Legends of the Bantu (1933)

ambundu_nzambi.name: Holds ultimate authority over rainfall, life and health
ambundu_nzambi.notes: Though distant, Nzambi remains the source of rain and of the life-force; petitions for these may be addressed to him even where mediation runs through the nkisi and ancestors.

sources.reference: Karl Laman, The Kongo (1953-68)

anglosaxon_beowulf.name: Hand-grip with the strength of thirty men
anglosaxon_beowulf.notes: The poet says Beowulf had in his hand-grip the strength of thirty men (lines 379-381), the power with which he tore off Grendel's arm.

sources.reference: Beowulf, ll. 379-381

anglosaxon_beowulf.name: Endures days swimming the sea in mail among sea-monsters
anglosaxon_beowulf.notes: In the boyhood swimming contest with Breca he is borne by the waves, slays nine niceras (sea-beasts) with his sword, and comes ashore in Finland (ll. 506-581).

sources.reference: Beowulf, ll. 506-581 (Unferth flyting and Beowulf's reply)

anglosaxon_hygd.name: Weaves peace and dispenses treasure as queen of the Geats
anglosaxon_hygd.notes: Daughter of Hæreth, she is the model young queen — wise, gracious, free-handed with gifts to the hall — set against the cautionary tyrant-queen Modthryth.

sources.reference: Beowulf, ll. 1925-1962 (Hygd and the Modthryth digression)

anglosaxon_hygd.name: Offers Beowulf the throne over her own son
anglosaxon_hygd.notes: After Hygelac's death Hygd offers Beowulf the hoard and kingdom, doubting her young son Heardred could hold it against foreign foes; Beowulf declines and supports Heardred.

sources.reference: Beowulf, ll. 2369-2376

anglosaxon_hygelac.name: Lord and ring-giver of the Geats, uncle and patron of Beowulf
anglosaxon_hygelac.notes: King of the Geats who rewards Beowulf with land, a hall and a great heirloom sword after the Grendel exploits; his maternal kinship to Beowulf grounds the hero's loyalty.

sources.reference: Beowulf, ll. 2190-2199

anglosaxon_hygelac.name: Leads the fatal raid on the Frisian/Frankish coast
anglosaxon_hygelac.notes: His historically anchored raid (the Chlochilaicus expedition, c. 516-521 CE) ends in his death; Beowulf escapes by swimming home with thirty war-corslets.

sources.reference: Gregory of Tours, Decem Libri Historiarum (History of the Franks) III.3; Beowulf, ll. 1202-1214, 2354-2366

anglosaxon_haethcyn.name: Accidentally slays his elder brother Herebeald with a misaimed shaft
anglosaxon_haethcyn.notes: The unintended kin-slaying of Herebeald brings his father Hrethel to fatal grief, a sorrow likened to a father's for a hanged son.

sources.reference: Beowulf, ll. 2435-2443

anglosaxon_heardred.name: Shelters the Swedish exiles Eanmund and Eadgils, drawing Onela's war
anglosaxon_heardred.notes: As young king of the Geats under Beowulf's regency, his harbouring of the rebel Scylfing princes brings the Swedish king Onela down on him; he is killed and Beowulf succeeds.

sources.reference: Beowulf, ll. 2379-2390

anglosaxon_nithhad.name: Captures and hamstrings the smith Wayland, forcing him to forge
anglosaxon_nithhad.notes: Níðhad seizes the master-smith, has his sinews cut to hobble him, and sets him to work on an island — the act Wayland avenges.

sources.reference: Deor, ll. 1-13; Völundarkviða (Poetic Edda)

anglosaxon_ecgtheow.name: Slays Heatholaf of the Wylfings and is sheltered by Hrothgar
anglosaxon_ecgtheow.notes: His killing of Heatholaf begins a feud; the Danish king Hrothgar receives him and settles it with wergild, founding the bond of gratitude Beowulf later repays.

sources.reference: Beowulf, ll. 459-472

anglosaxon_widia.name: Delivers Theodric from the giants in Widsith
anglosaxon_widia.notes: In Widsith, Wudga (Widia) and his companion Hama win renown; later tradition makes him a champion of the Dietrich/Þiðrekr cycle who wields his father's sword Mimming.

sources.reference: Widsith, ll. 124-130; Waldere fragment II

anglosaxon_wiglaf.name: Alone stands by Beowulf against the dragon
anglosaxon_wiglaf.notes: When the other retainers flee, the young Wægmunding Wiglaf goes into the fire to aid his lord, helps deal the dragon its death-wound, and receives Beowulf's dying words and bequest.

anglosaxon_eostre.name: Receives feasts in her month at the turn of spring
anglosaxon_eostre.notes: Bede records that feasts were held in her honour in Eosturmonath (≈April), the month later lending its name to the Paschal season.

sources.reference: Bede, De temporum ratione (725 CE), ch. 15 'De mensibus Anglorum'

anglosaxon_frig.name: Presides over love, marriage and the bonds of the household
anglosaxon_frig.notes: Reconstructed from her Norse cognate Frigg and her survival in Frīgedæg (Friday) and place-names; chief goddess of married love and the home.

sources.reference: Philip A. Shaw, Pagan Goddesses in the Early Germanic World: Eostre, Hreda and the Cult of Matrons (2011)

arabian_al_uzza.name: Grants victory and protection in war
arabian_al_uzza.notes: Invoked by the Quraysh as a war-protector; at Uhud the cry 'We have al-'Uzza and you have no 'Uzza' is reported, and she was sought for aid in battle.

sources.reference: Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam (Book of Idols); Ibn Hisham, Sira (Battle of Uhud)

arabian_al_uzza.name: Delivers oracular communications at her shrine
arabian_al_uzza.notes: At the sanctuary of Buss in the valley of Hurad at Nakhlah, the people received oracular responses from her.

sources.reference: Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam (Book of Idols)

arabian_allat.name: Grants rain, fertility and the abundance of the earth
arabian_allat.notes: As a great mother-goddess of the harvest she was petitioned for fertility and prosperity across pre-Islamic Arabia.

sources.reference: J. F. Healey, The Religion of the Nabataeans (2001); Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam

arabian_allat.name: Shelters petitioners within her inviolable sanctuary
arabian_allat.notes: Her haram at al-Ta'if was a place of refuge where bloodshed and hunting were forbidden within its bounds.

sources.reference: Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam (Book of Idols)

arabian_antara.name: Peerless prowess in single combat and the charge
arabian_antara.notes: Celebrated for breaking enemy lines lance and sword in hand from horseback; his Mu'allaqa boasts of plunging into the thick of battle and emerging victorious.

sources.reference: The Mu'allaqa of 'Antara ibn Shaddad (in the Mu'allaqat)

arabian_antara.name: Mastery of heroic and amatory verse
arabian_antara.notes: Composer of one of the seven Mu'allaqat, weaving valor with his love for 'Abla; his ode is a canonical model of pre-Islamic eloquence.

sources.reference: The Mu'allaqa of 'Antara ibn Shaddad

arabian_hatim_al_tai.name: Boundless hospitality and self-sacrificing generosity
arabian_hatim_al_tai.notes: The proverbial paragon of Arab jud (generosity): when caught without provisions for a guest, he slaughters his own prized horse to feed him.

sources.reference: Kitab al-Aghani (al-Isfahani); Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Hatem Ta'i'

arabian_hatim_al_tai.name: Hospitality that continues even from beyond the grave
arabian_hatim_al_tai.notes: In the famous tale, travellers who jokingly claim his hospitality at his tomb are fed when one of their camels sickens and must be slaughtered, and the maidens of his grave are heard mourning.

sources.reference: Alf Layla wa-Layla (The Thousand and One Nights), 'Hatim of the tribe of Tayy'

arabian_adi_ibn_hatim.name: Leads the tribe of Tayyi' across the coming of Islam
arabian_adi_ibn_hatim.notes: Inheriting his father's leadership, he held the chieftaincy and the customary fourth-share of raid spoils before converting to Islam in 9 AH and becoming a Companion.

sources.reference: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab al-Tabaqat al-Kabir; Ibn Hisham, Sira

arabian_adi_ibn_hatim.name: Appointed by Muhammad to collect the alms of Tayyi' and Banu Asad
arabian_adi_ibn_hatim.notes: After conversion the Prophet entrusted him with gathering the sadaqa (zakat) of his people; he later fought in the Ridda wars and the conquests of Iraq.

sources.reference: Ibn Sa'd, Kitab al-Tabaqat al-Kabir

apache_white_painted_woman.name: Survives the world-flood sealed in an abalone shell
apache_white_painted_woman.notes: White Painted Woman rides out the primordial flood inside an abalone (or other) shell, then climbs a mountain where the Sun impregnates her.

sources.reference: Morris E. Opler, An Apache Life-Way (1941); Myths and Tales of the Chiricahua Apache Indians (1942)

apache_child_of_the_water.name: Endures the Sun's ordeals to be acknowledged as his son
apache_child_of_the_water.notes: Travelling to his father the Sun, Child of the Water survives tests of fire, cold and arrows and is given power and weapons against the monsters.

sources.reference: Morris E. Opler, Myths and Tales of the Chiricahua Apache Indians (1942)

andamanese_maia_lircitmo.name: Steals fire from the sleeping creator and brings it to the ancestors
andamanese_maia_lircitmo.notes: The Kingfisher (Maia, 'Sir') takes a brand from Bilik (or from the camp of the dead) while he sleeps; struck by the brand Bilik hurls, he is scorched on the neck but delivers fire to the people at Wota-emi.

sources.reference: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown, The Andaman Islanders (1922), ch. on myths and legends

andamanese_tarai.name: Sends the south-west monsoon with his heavy breathing
andamanese_tarai.notes: Tarai, long-legged and short-bodied, lives on a (now-submerged) island; when he sleeps his deep breaths make the wind of the wet-season monsoon.

sources.reference: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown, The Andaman Islanders (1922)

andamanese_tomo.name: Receives and teaches the arts of living to the first people
andamanese_tomo.notes: As the first man, Tomo is taught by the creator how to make fire, hunt, fish and build, and passes these arts to his descendants, the ancestors of the present race.

sources.reference: E. H. Man, On the Aboriginal Inhabitants of the Andaman Islands (1883); A. R. Radcliffe-Brown, The Andaman Islanders (1922)

arabian_allat.name: The lion of Allat (colossal stone lion of her sanctuary)

sources.reference: Palmyrene lion sculpture from the Temple of Allat, Palmyra (1st c. CE)

andamanese_biliku.name: Spider's web (with which she is said to have spun the world)

sources.reference: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown, The Andaman Islanders (1922)

sources.reference: Old English glosses rendering Mars by Tig/Tiw

anglosaxon_seaxneat.name: Renunciation in the Old Saxon Baptismal Vow

term.value: end ec forsacho allum dioboles uuercum and uuordum, Thunaer ende Uuoden ende Saxnote

anglosaxon_seaxneat.notes: His former cult is attested negatively: converts to Christianity were required to forsake him by name alongside Woden and Thunaer, marking him as one of the three chief gods of the continental Saxons; among the English he survives as divine ancestor of the East Saxon (Essex) kings.

sources.reference: Old Saxon Baptismal Vow (Vatican, Pal. Lat. 577)

ambundu_kianda.name: Luanda Island Feast (Festa da Ilha de Luanda)
ambundu_kianda.notes: Annual feast on the Ilha de Luanda honouring Kianda, protectress of fishermen; offerings of food and cloth are cast into the sea to keep peace with the waters and ensure the catch.

sources.reference: Heli Chatelain, Folk-Tales of Angola (1894); ethnography of the Ilha de Luanda

arabian_al_uzza.name: Pilgrimage and sacrifice at Nakhlah
arabian_al_uzza.notes: Worshippers journeyed to her grove of three trees at Nakhlah near the shrine of Buss, brought gifts and sought her favour through sacrifice and oracular consultation; the cult was suppressed when Khalid ibn al-Walid felled the trees (8 AH/630 CE).

sources.reference: Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam (Book of Idols)

arabian_allat.name: Sacrifice at the haram of al-Ta'if
arabian_allat.notes: Her cubic white stone at al-Ta'if, kept by the Banu 'Attab of Thaqif, stood within an inviolable precinct where hunting and bloodshed were forbidden; pilgrims circled and offered to her until the shrine was destroyed by al-Mughira ibn Shu'ba.

sources.reference: Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam (Book of Idols)

anglosaxon_eostre.name: Feasts of Eosturmonath
anglosaxon_eostre.notes: Bede reports that in the heathen past feasts were held in her honour during the month named for her, the inherited name later transferred to the Christian Paschal season.

sources.reference: Bede, De temporum ratione, ch. 15

anglosaxon_thunor.name: Thunor place-cult and hammer amulets
anglosaxon_thunor.notes: Attested indirectly by some twelve English place-names (e.g. Þunres lēah 'Thunderley', Þunres feld 'Thunderfield') marking groves and fields sacred to him, and by Þorr-style hammer amulets in Anglo-Saxon and Jutish graves (e.g. Gilton, Kent).

sources.reference: Margaret Gelling, Signposts to the Past (1978); David Wilson, Anglo-Saxon Paganism (1992)

anglosaxon_woden.name: Dynastic descent and place-cult
anglosaxon_woden.notes: Most Anglo-Saxon royal houses traced their pedigree to Woden, and his name marks sacred sites in place-names such as Wodnesbeorg ('Woden's barrow') and Wansdyke (Wodnes dic); his cult is otherwise attested by his renunciation in the Old Saxon Baptismal Vow.

sources.reference: Anglo-Saxon Chronicle royal genealogies; Margaret Gelling, Signposts to the Past (1978)

arabian_hatim_al_tai.name: Veneration at the grave of Hatim
arabian_hatim_al_tai.notes: Not a cult of worship but a site of legend: his hilltop tomb was marked by two stone troughs (recalling the pots from which he fed the poor) and statues of mourning maidens; travellers camped there expecting his posthumous hospitality.

sources.reference: Encyclopaedia Iranica, 'Hatem Ta'i'; Alf Layla wa-Layla

attributes.name: Sun/fire shield-emblem
attributes.notes: As the twin fathered by (or aligned with) the Sun, Killer of Enemies is marked by fire and sun symbols, shown as a shield emblem or flicker-feather headdress distinguishing him from his water-aligned brother.

sources.reference: Morris E. Opler, 'Athapaskan Culture Heroes: Killer-of-Enemies and Child-of-the-Water' (1938)

attributes.name: Water/moon emblem
attributes.notes: The twin aligned with water (and the moon/rain) bears water symbols opposite his brother's fire emblem; in Chiricahua and Mescalero tradition he is the dominant of the two heroes.

sources.reference: Morris E. Opler, 'Athapaskan Culture Heroes' (1938); Myths and Tales of the Chiricahua Apache Indians (1942)

attributes.name: Bone amulets worn against the sea-dead
attributes.notes: Amulets fashioned from the bones of dead kin were worn to ward off the dangerous spirits of the dead.

sources.reference: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown, The Andaman Islanders (1922)

attributes.name: Bone amulets worn against the forest-dead
attributes.notes: Bone amulets of dead relatives were believed to repel the lau and the sickness they bring.

sources.reference: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown, The Andaman Islanders (1922)

attributes.name: Nine glory-twigs (wuldortanas)
attributes.notes: In the Nine Herbs Charm Woden smites the serpent into nine pieces with nine wuldortanas ('glory-twigs'), his instruments of healing and charm-magic.

sources.reference: Nine Herbs Charm (Lacnunga, BL Harley 585)

attributes.name: Concealing hood/mask
attributes.notes: Implied by his byname Grim ('the masked/hooded one'); the disguised wanderer of the Germanic Wodan/Óðinn type.

sources.reference: cf. Old Norse Grímnir; English Grim- place-names

attributes.name: Hammer
attributes.notes: His weapon and emblem, worn as a protective pendant in the Anglo-Saxon and Jutish hammer-amulets paralleling the Norse Mjöllnir cult.

sources.reference: Hammer amulets, Jutish cemetery at Gilton, Kent; David Wilson, Anglo-Saxon Paganism (1992)

attributes.name: Thunder and lightning
attributes.notes: The thunder itself (Old English þunor) is his manifestation, like that of his cognate Þórr.

sources.reference: Old English vocabulary; cf. Thor

attributes.name: The Tīr rune (↑)
attributes.notes: The arrow-like 'T'-rune named for the god is described in the Old English Rune Poem as a sure guide, ever keeping faith, and was inscribed on weapons for victory.

sources.reference: Old English Rune Poem

attributes.name: Sacred stone (baetyl) and trees
attributes.notes: Worshipped aniconically in three sacred acacia/samura trees and an associated stone at Nakhlah.

sources.reference: Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam
Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam (the three trees at Nakhlah)
Nabataean/Sinaitic equation of al-'Uzza with Aphrodite/Venus

attributes.name: Cubic white granite stone
attributes.notes: At al-Ta'if she was venerated in the form of a square white stone within her temple precinct.

sources.reference: Ibn al-Kalbi, Kitab al-Asnam

attributes.name: Helmet, spear and aegis (Palmyrene Athena type)
attributes.notes: In Palmyrene sculpture of the Roman period she is shown armed as Athena, with helmet, spear and aegis.

sources.reference: Palmyrene reliefs of Allat as Athena (1st-2nd c. CE)
Colossal lion of the Temple of Allat, Palmyra, holding a gazelle

sacredAnimals.name: Gazelle (sheltered between the lion's paws, symbol of her mercy)

sources.reference: Lion of Allat, Palmyra

attributes.name: Abalone shell
attributes.notes: Her emblem and refuge: she rode out the flood in an abalone shell, and Apache girls wear an abalone-shell pendant on the brow in the Sunrise Ceremony she instituted.

sources.reference: Morris E. Opler, An Apache Life-Way (1941)

attributes.name: Scarlet throat-patch
attributes.notes: The kingfisher's bright red neck-feathers are said to mark the burn where Bilik's thrown firebrand scorched him as he carried off the fire.

sources.reference: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown, The Andaman Islanders (1922)
A. R. Radcliffe-Brown, The Andaman Islanders (1922)
A. R. Radcliffe-Brown, The Andaman Islanders (1922)

sacredAnimals.name: Cicada (killing or disturbing it rouses her wrath)

sources.reference: A. R. Radcliffe-Brown, The Andaman Islanders (1922)

attributes.name: Smith's tongs and forge
attributes.notes: His defining attribute on the Franks Casket front panel: hobbled at his anvil, gripping with tongs the skull-cup made from Niðhad's son.

sources.reference: Franks Casket (early 8th c., British Museum), front panel

attributes.name: Feathered flying-gear
attributes.notes: The wings (flygil) he forges from birds' feathers to escape his captivity, alluded to in the bird-catching figure on the Franks Casket.

sources.reference: Völundarkviða; Þiðreks saga; Franks Casket

attributes.name: Grendel's torn-off arm and hand
attributes.notes: Hung up under Heorot's gabled roof as the trophy and proof of Beowulf's bare-handed victory.
